---
title: "Forwards and Futures — Agree on a Price for Later"
description: "An investment science derivatives idea explained through a single small numerical story."
---

## Imagine this situation

**A bicycle costs 100 today. You want to guarantee the purchase price one year from now. What should a simple forward delivery price be?**

An idealised forward contract promises an asset in the future in exchange for a predetermined payment. A fair **delivery price** is not the same thing as the contract's **current value**.

## Translate the story into mathematics

$$
F_0=S_0(1+r)^T
$$

**What each symbol means:** F_0 is the fair forward delivery price agreed today for delivery at time T; S_0 is today's underlying spot price; r is the annual risk-free financing rate; T counts years. This formula assumes no income, dividends or storage benefits/costs, and compatible financing conventions.

**Put the actual numbers in:** If the bicycle (or a non-dividend-paying investment asset) costs 100 now, financing is 5% for one year, and there is no income or storage cost, the forward delivery price is 100×1.05=**105**. You can replicate delivery by borrowing 100 today, buying the item and repaying 105 next year.

## The idea behind the equation

If a guaranteed forward delivery cost were much above 105 in the idealised setting, a trader could buy/finance and sell forward; if much below, reverse transactions might be possible subject to short-selling and borrowing rules. Both legs create the same future asset position.

## Compute it without a large library

~~~python
from finance_lab import forward_delivery_price
print(forward_delivery_price(100,.05,1)) # 105
~~~

Where applicable, the numerical expression is also available in the [tested finance calculation lab](../examples/index.qmd).

## What changes in real markets?

The fair **forward delivery price** is 105, but an at-market newly written forward can have roughly ZERO initial value. Later its value changes with spot price and discount rates. Futures are typically exchange-traded and marked to market daily, so futures and forwards are not identical when rate correlations and collateral details matter.
